title: Cranberry Sauce

drivers.name: Store closure (Monday)
drivers.evidence: Store closed Monday; historical data shows no closure effects, but 1/7 of sales days lost. Estimated 20% demand reduction.

adjustment.analysis: The target week has no events, but the store is closed Monday, reducing sales days. A 2.1% price increase is minor and not expected to significantly impact demand. The classical uplift model suggests +23% for Thanksgiving prep, but this week is 6 weeks before Thanksgiving—too early for seasonal ramp. Past Thanksgiving prep weeks show noise-adjusted lift of x1.23, but that’s not applicable here. The recent price increase to $2.91 (vs $2.85) has no observed effect in the data (2026-09-28: 22 units, x1.0). Store closure on Monday likely reduces sales by ~20% (1/7 of week), but no prior closure data exists. No promotion or price drop. The baseline already includes trend and seasonality. Adjust only for the closure, with low confidence due to lack of evidence.

brief:
PRODUCT: Cranberry Sauce | category Grocery | Store #12 (Austin, TX)
TARGET WEEK: 2026-11-16 to 2026-11-22 (6 weeks after the last week with sales data)

KNOWN PLAN FOR THE TARGET WEEK:
  events: none
  shelf price: 2.91 (+2.1% vs regular price 2.85)
  planner notes: Store closed Monday for renovation

STATISTICAL BASELINE (exponential smoothing of recent sales; it ignores events, promotions and prices):
  median 9.0 | 5%-95%: 0.0 - 20.6 | 10%-90%: 1.3 - 17.9

In the evidence below, 'vs baseline' = actual units / what this same baseline predicted for that week.
It is the multiplier that would have been right, so it maps directly onto median_multiplier.
This product's ordinary weeks already swing about +/-81% around the baseline, so a past effect smaller than that, seen only a few times, is mostly noise. The
'noise-adjusted estimate' is the effect shrunk toward x1.0 for that noise and the number of sightings.
